q: You are three days out of Las Palmas on the ARC route, in the trade-wind belt. Why does the wind blow from the NE and not straight from the N?
a: The Earth's rotation turns it to the right
o: The Canary Current drags it to the west
The Sahara's heat pulls it in from the east
The Azores High spins it anticlockwise
why: Coriolis turns moving air to the right in the north: the flow back to the equator becomes the NE trade.

fig.title: Leaving Gran Canaria, late November
lines: Air flows south towards the equator

q: You left Madeira for the Cape Verdes and the wind has died. Why is there so little wind here?
a: Air from the Hadley cell sinks here under a high
o: Air rises here and the cloud smothers the wind
The trades and the westerlies cancel each other
The cold Canary Current stops the air moving
why: Air lifted at the ITCZ sinks again near 30°: a belt of high pressure, light winds and dry air — the horse latitudes.

fig.title: Becalmed at 30°N 25°W
lines: Sky clear, air dry, sea glassy

q: You leave Santa Cruz for Hiva Oa on the Pacific Puddle Jump. What wind do you expect for most of the passage?
a: The SE trade, on the port quarter
o: The NE trade, on the starboard quarter
The westerlies, close-hauled all the way
The calms and squalls of the doldrums
why: South of the ITCZ the SE trade blows: from about 135° on a course of 250° it is on the port quarter.

q: You plan the run south from the Cape Verdes to Brazil. Where do you expect to meet the doldrums?
a: Around 0–5°N, the ITCZ at its farthest south
o: Around 10–12°N, where it lies in August
Right off the Cape Verdes, at about 15°N
South of the equator, around 5–10°S
why: The ITCZ follows the Sun with a lag: in the Atlantic it lies nearest the equator in Feb–Apr and farthest north in Aug–Sep.

fig.title: Mindelo to Salvador, 1 March
lines: Course south, crossing the equator at 28°W

q: You leave Bermuda for Horta in early June, and the Azores High lies across the rhumb line, as here. Which way do you go?
a: North of the centre, where the westerlies blow
o: Straight through the centre, the shortest way
South of the centre, along its southern side
Wait in Bermuda until the high has moved away
why: Round a northern high the wind turns clockwise: westerlies on its north side, easterlies on its south side, calm in the middle.

q: You are planning the passage home from Hawaii to California. Which route do you take?
a: North on starboard tack, round the top of the high, then east
o: The rhumb line, beating NE into the trade all the way
South of the high in the trade, then up the coast
Through the middle of the high, motoring the calms
why: Clockwise flow round the high: sail north across the trade, reach the westerlies above it, then run east to the coast.
ref: Subtropical highs — the North Pacific High

q: You are two days out of Cape Town, north-east of the South Atlantic High, steering for St Helena. What wind do you expect?
a: SE, from almost dead astern
o: NW, almost on the nose
NE, on the starboard beam
SW, on the port beam
why: A southern high turns anticlockwise: on its NE side the air flows to the NW — the SE trade, astern on a course of 320°.
ref: Subtropical highs — the St Helena High

q: You plan to run east along 40°S across the Indian Ocean. What weather do you prepare the boat for?
a: Fair westerlies, with a gale as each low passes
o: A steady SE trade under settled skies
Mostly calms under a permanent high
Easterlies on the nose most of the way
why: No land stops the Southern Ocean lows: the roaring forties give strong westerlies and a gale every few days.

fig.title: Cape Town to Fremantle along 40°S
lines: Pilot chart: gales 10 % of the time

q: Your 24 m expedition yacht leaves Iceland for Svalbard, north of the storm track of the westerlies. Which prevailing wind do you plan for near 75°N?
a: Easterlies blowing out of the polar high
o: Westerlies, stronger the farther north
The NE trade, steady at force 4
The SW monsoon of high summer
why: Beyond about 60° cold air flows out of the polar high and Coriolis turns it west: the polar easterlies.

q: It is early June in Galle and a crew member suggests leaving now for Oman. What does the pilot chart for June tell you?
a: The SW monsoon has set in: F6–7 on the nose and a rough sea all the way
o: The NE monsoon is still blowing: a fast run with the wind astern
It is the transition: light airs, motoring most of the way
The monsoon is over: easy trade-wind sailing to the west
why: From June to September the SW monsoon blows hard across the Arabian Sea: a westbound passage is a beat into a big sea.

fig.title: Pilot chart, June: Arabian Sea
lines: Wind rose: SW, F6–7 most of the month

q: You are ready to cross to the Bahamas. When do you go?
a: Tomorrow evening, once the northerly has eased
o: Now, to get across ahead of the front
Tomorrow morning, in the N 20–25 kn
Tonight, while the front is passing
why: Wind against a 3 kn current raises short, steep, breaking seas: never cross the Gulf Stream with a wind from the north.

fig.title: Fort Lauderdale, 1800
lines: Bimini: 45 M east, across the Gulf Stream
Gulf Stream setting N at 3 kn
Cold front due 2000, then N 20–25 kn

q: You are running west in the trade wind. What is your run over the ground in 24 hours?
why: The North Equatorial Current sets west with you: (6.5 + 0.5) × 24 = 168 M over the ground.
ref: Ocean currents — the North Equatorial Current

fig.title: ARC, day 10, 16°N 45°W
lines: Pilot chart: current 0.5 kn, setting W

q: You are waiting to sail down the South African coast. What do you decide?
a: Go now: in port about 6 h before the change
o: Wait, then go with the SW wind behind the front
Go now and stay in the current when it turns SW
Go as the front passes: the current calms the sea
why: A SW gale against the 2–4 kn Agulhas raises huge, steep seas: sail in the NE window and be in port before the change.

fig.title: Richards Bay, bound SW for East London
lines: 300 M: about 30 h with the current
Now: NE 15–20 kn for the next 36 h
Then a cold front: SW 35–40 kn

q: Your crew expected tropical heat this close to the equator. What explains this weather?
a: The cold Humboldt Current flowing north
o: The warm Kuroshio flowing south
The Canary Current crossing from Africa
The ITCZ lying overhead in February
why: The Humboldt (Peru) Current brings cold water north along South America: cool, stable air, low cloud and almost no rain.

fig.title: Callao, Peru, 12°S, February
lines: Low grey cloud, no rain for months

q: You are sailing north-east along the coast of Japan. Where do you put the boat?
a: In the Kuroshio, wind and current both NE-going
o: Inshore of it, out of the current's set
Well offshore, south of the current
In the Kuroshio only if the wind turns NE
why: The Kuroshio is Japan's Gulf Stream: with a SW wind ride its axis for 2–4 kn more; never stay in it in a NE blow.

fig.title: Amami to Tokyo Bay, May, 450 M NE
lines: Pilot chart: Kuroshio sets NE, 2–4 kn

q: On a circumnavigation you will hear storm warnings in each of these places. What does each forecast call a tropical revolving storm?
a: Hurricane, typhoon, cyclone, cyclone
o: Hurricane, hurricane, typhoon, cyclone
Typhoon, hurricane, cyclone, typhoon
Cyclone, typhoon, hurricane, hurricane
why: Atlantic and NE Pacific: hurricane; NW Pacific: typhoon; Indian Ocean and South Pacific: (tropical) cyclone.

fig.title: One kind of storm, four oceans
lines: D: the Bay of Bengal, November

q: Your crew want to stay in the Caribbean until October. Which plan fits the North Atlantic hurricane season?
a: Leave the belt by June; the season runs to November
o: Leave by September; the season is only Aug–Sep
Stay; storms are rare before October
Stay; hurricanes never reach the Leewards
why: The North Atlantic season runs 1 June – 30 November, peaking Aug–Oct: be out of the hurricane belt by June.

fig.title: Antigua, end of April
lines: Plan: cruise the Leewards into autumn
Pilot charts Aug–Oct: TRS tracks across them
Insurer: no named-storm cover in season

q: What do you tell the crew about the South Pacific cyclone season?
a: It runs November–April: be in New Zealand by then
o: It runs June–November, as in the Caribbean
It runs May–October, in the southern winter
There is none: no cyclones form south of the equator
why: Southern-hemisphere cyclones come in the southern summer, Nov–Apr: most boats leave Tonga for New Zealand in Oct–Nov.

fig.title: Neiafu, Tonga, mid-October
lines: Next stop on the plan: New Zealand in May

q: Which months carry the highest risk of a cyclone on this crossing?
a: May and Oct–Nov, as the monsoon changes
o: July–August, at the height of the SW monsoon
January–February, in the NE monsoon
None: the Bay of Bengal has no cyclones
why: North Indian Ocean cyclones peak at the monsoon changes, Apr–Jun and Oct–Dec; the strong SW monsoon's shear stops most in Jul–Aug.

fig.title: Galle to Phuket, across the Bay of Bengal
lines: Sea warm enough for storms all year
Months being discussed: Jan, May, Aug, Nov

q: Each area shows a cluster of thunderstorms. Which one could grow into a hurricane?
a: B: warm sea, far enough from the equator
o: A: the warmest sea of the four
C: the farthest north, in the westerlies
D: in the South Atlantic, in its winter
why: A TRS needs a sea of about 26.5 °C or more and Coriolis spin, so at least 5° from the equator: only B has both.

q: You have hired a weather router for the crossing. Who decides each day when to reef and which way to go?
a: You: the router advises, the skipper decides
o: The router: they see the full model output
The router, unless the GRIB disagrees
Whoever is on watch when the e-mail comes
why: A router sees models, not your sky, sea and barometer: the advice is one input, and the decisions stay with the skipper.

fig.title: Routing service, Canaries to Antigua
lines: Advice from the latest model runs

q: You are three days from Martinique. What do you make of these signs?
a: A TRS may lie to the ESE: log the glass hourly
o: A cold front is coming down from the north
A normal trade-wind day: carry on as before
The ITCZ is moving north towards you
why: A long swell and cirrus radiating from one point are the first signs of a TRS, often before the barometer moves.

fig.title: 15°N 55°W, early September
lines: NE trade 15 kn, as for a week
New long swell from ESE, period 14 s
Cirrus streaks fanning out from the ESE
Barometer 1012 hPa, normal for the hour

q: You log this reading in the hurricane season. How far below normal is it, and what does it mean?
a: 4.5 hPa below normal for 1000: suspect a TRS
o: 1.5 hPa below normal: within the daily swing
3.0 hPa below the mean: only the daily swing
No fall at all once the daily swing is allowed
why: Normal at 1000 = 1013 + 1.5 = 1014.5; 1014.5 − 1010 = 4.5 hPa. 3 hPa or more below normal in the tropics warns of a TRS.

fig.title: Barometer at 1000 local, 16°N
lines: Pilot chart mean for the month: 1013 hPa

q: A crew member is alarmed by a fall of 3 hPa in six hours. What do you tell them?
a: Normal: the glass peaks near 1000 and dips near 1600
o: A TRS is near: 3 hPa in six hours is the sign
A cold front is coming: expect a sharp veer
The barometer is faulty: tropical pressure never moves
why: Tropical pressure has a twice-daily tide of about 3 hPa: highs near 1000 and 2200, lows near 0400 and 1600.

q: Your crew say a hurricane heading NW will pass well west of Bermuda. What is its most likely path over the next few days?
a: It recurves north, then north-east, speeding up
o: It keeps going NW until it reaches the US coast
It turns west-south-west, back into the Caribbean
It stalls and fills where it is within a day
why: North Atlantic storms move W–NW round the high, then recurve N and NE into the westerlies, faster — often towards Bermuda.

q: The depression is north-west of you. Which path does a storm born here typically take?
a: West-south-west at first, then recurving south-east
o: West-north-west at first, then recurving north-east
East along 10°S at first, then turning north
South-west at first, then on to the west
why: Southern storms move west and poleward, then recurve S and SE into the westerlies: the mirror of the northern track.

q: This hurricane east of the Leeward Islands is moving west. Which side of it is the dangerous semicircle?
a: The north side, right of the track
o: The south side, left of the track
The west side, ahead of the centre
The east side, behind the centre
why: North of the equator it is the right-hand half, looking along the track: the storm's speed adds to the wind, which blows you into its path.

q: This cyclone north-east of Mauritius is moving south-west. Which side of it is the dangerous semicircle?
a: The south-east side, left of the track
o: The north-west side, right of the track
The south-west side, ahead of the centre
The north-east side, behind the centre
why: South of the equator the dangerous half is the left-hand one, looking along the track: on a SW track that is the SE side.

q: You face the wind to find the typhoon's centre. Roughly which way does it bear?
a: About 150°
o: About 290°
About 220°
About 040°
why: North of the equator, face the wind and the centre is on your right, about 10 points at first: 040° + 112° ≈ 150°.
ref: Tropical revolving storms — Buys Ballot's law

fig.title: South China Sea, typhoon warning
lines: Centre about 10 points (112°) from the wind

q: Sailing from Nouméa towards Brisbane, you need to know where the cyclone's centre lies. Which way does it bear from you?
a: About 220°
o: About 080°
About 150°
About 330°
why: South of the equator, face the wind and the low is on your left: 330° − 112° ≈ 220°.
ref: Tropical revolving storms — Buys Ballot's law

fig.title: Coral Sea, cyclone warning
lines: Centre about 10 points (112°) from the wind

q: You log the wind and barometer every two hours as the storm comes closer. Where are you relative to it?
a: In the dangerous semicircle: the wind is veering
o: In the navigable semicircle: the wind is backing
In the dangerous semicircle: the wind is backing
Right in its path: the wind is holding steady
why: E → ESE → SE turns clockwise, a veer: north of the equator a veering wind puts you in the right-hand, dangerous half.

q: The wind shifts like this as the hurricane approaches. What do you do?
a: Put the wind on the starboard quarter and run
o: Put the wind on the starboard bow, close-hauled
Put the wind on the port quarter and run
Heave to on port tack and wait for it to pass
why: NE → N is backing: the navigable half in the north. Run with the wind on the starboard quarter, away from the centre.

fig.title: Hurricane to the SE, moving NW

q: You have logged these over the last six hours in the South China Sea. What does it tell you, and what do you do?
a: On its track: run, wind on the starboard quarter
o: On its track: run, wind on the port quarter
Navigable half: hold your course and wait
Dangerous half: close-hauled, wind on starboard bow
why: A steady wind and a falling glass put you on the track; north of the equator run with the wind on the starboard quarter.

fig.title: Typhoon to the SE, moving NW
lines: Wind NE 7, direction steady for 6 h

q: Your plot puts you here, 150 M north of a hurricane that is moving west. Which action is right?
a: Close-hauled on starboard tack, wind on the starboard bow
o: Run with the wind on the starboard quarter
Close-hauled on port tack, wind on the port bow
Run with the wind on the port quarter
why: North of a westbound storm is its right, dangerous half: in the north keep the wind on the starboard bow and claw away.

q: You log these as a cyclone approaches Tonga. Where are you, and what do you do?
a: Dangerous half: close-hauled on port tack
o: Navigable half: run, wind on the port quarter
Dangerous half: close-hauled on starboard tack
Navigable half: run, wind on the starboard quarter
why: SE → E → NE is backing; south of the equator that is the left-hand, dangerous half: keep the wind on the port bow.

q: A cyclone is tracking west across the Coral Sea, and the plot puts you on its north side, as here. What do you do?
a: Run with the wind on the port quarter
o: Close-hauled on port tack, wind on the port bow
Run with the wind on the starboard quarter
Close-hauled on starboard tack, wind on the starboard bow
why: In the south the right-hand half of a westbound storm, its north side, is navigable: run with the wind on the port quarter.

q: You are south-west of Fiji with these readings. Where are you, and which action do you take?
a: On its track: run, wind on the port quarter
o: On its track: run, wind on the starboard quarter
Navigable half: hold your course and wait
Dangerous half: close-hauled, wind on the port bow
why: A steady wind and a falling glass: you are on the track. South of the equator run with the wind on the port quarter.

fig.title: Cyclone to the NE, moving SW
lines: Wind SE 7, direction steady for 5 h

q: You plot the advisory using the mariner's 1-2-3 rule. What radius round the 48-hour forecast position do you keep out of?
why: 1-2-3 rule: add 100, 200, 300 M of forecast error at 24, 48, 72 h to the 34-kn radius: 120 + 200 = 320 M.

q: Using the 1-2-3 rule, is your plan safe?
a: No: you would be inside the 350 M zone
o: Yes: you would be outside the 150 M radius
Yes: the 48-h zone is only 250 M
Yes: you stay more than 200 M from the centre
why: At 48 h: 150 + 200 = 350 M; at 280 M your DR is inside the zone — re-route now, while the storm is still far off.

fig.title: Storm plot, 48 h ahead
lines: Your DR in 48 h: 280 M from it

q: If you stay where you are, how long before the 34-knot winds reach you?
a: About 15 h
o: About 24 h
About 32 h
About 9 h
why: (330 − 120) ÷ 14 = 15 h: the gale arrives with the edge of the 34-kn radius, long before the centre.

q: How far from the centre are you after 24 hours?
a: About 201 M
o: About 72 M
About 144 M
About 216 M
why: The storm runs 288 M to 72 M E of your start; you run 144 M SW: √(173.8² + 101.8²) ≈ 201 M, clear of the 34-kn winds.

fig.title: Hurricane 360 M due east of you
lines: You run 225° at 6 kn for 24 h

q: You are north of the equator. What wind do you expect at your position?
a: 34 kn or more: inside the NE radius
o: Under 34 kn: outside the 60 M SW radius
Under 34 kn: beyond the 105 M mean radius
64 kn or more: inside the hurricane core
why: The radii are given per quadrant and are widest on the right of the track in the north: 130 M NE is inside 150 M.

fig.title: Advisory: 34-kn wind radii
lines: You: 130 M NE of the centre

q: How long before the squall reaches you?
a: About 45 min
o: About 24 min
About 16 min
About 51 min
why: It closes at 15 − 7 = 8 kn: 6 ÷ 8 = 0.75 h = 45 min — time to reef before it arrives, not in it.

fig.title: Trade winds, night, 0230
lines: Stars vanishing under a line of cloud
Squalls move with the trade at 15 kn
You: running at 7 kn, poled-out genoa

q: You are crossing from Newport to the Azores, and this depression is passing north of you. How does the wind change when its cold front comes through?
a: It veers from SW to NW, in squalls
o: It backs from SW to SE, with drizzle
It veers from NW to NE, then falls calm
It backs from NW to SW, the glass falling
why: North of the equator a cold front brings a sharp veer, SW to W or NW, squalls, then a rising glass and clearer air.
ref: Depressions — fronts on an ocean crossing

q: You are running east to Fremantle. How does the wind shift as the front passes?
a: It backs from NW to SW, in squalls
o: It veers from NW to NE, with rain
It holds NW and slowly eases
It drops to a calm, and fog sets in
why: Lows turn clockwise in the south: NW ahead of a cold front, SW behind it — a back, with squalls and a rising glass.
ref: Depressions — fronts on an ocean crossing

fig.title: Southern Indian Ocean, 40°S
lines: Low passing to the south, moving E

q: You are eastbound across the North Atlantic, and this faster low will overtake you. You can alter north or south now. Which do you choose?
a: South, so its centre passes north of you
o: North, so its centre passes south of you
Neither: heave to and let it pass over you
North, to meet its warm front sooner
why: With the centre passing north of you the wind runs SW → W → NW, all fair eastbound; north of it you meet easterlies.
ref: Depressions — fronts on an ocean crossing

q: The GRIB file and the advisory disagree about tomorrow. Which do you plan by?
a: The advisory: a GRIB blunts a small, intense storm
o: The GRIB: it is the newer and finer data
An average of the two forecasts
The GRIB, unless the barometer has fallen
why: A GRIB is raw model output on a coarse grid: it underplays a tropical storm's winds and track. Trust the forecaster's advisory.
ref: Weather information — GRIB and its limits

fig.title: Two forecasts for tomorrow
lines: GRIB (GFS, 0.5°): NE 20 kn on your route
NHC: moving W at 12 kn, 34-kn radius 100 M

q: Why has the NAVTEX gone quiet, and where do you now get the official high-seas forecast?
a: Out of range: SafetyNET and HF weatherfax
o: Out of range: VHF Ch 16 every four hours
Faulty set: retune it to 490 kHz
No warnings issued: keep waiting for NAVTEX
why: NAVTEX reaches only about 300–400 M from its station: offshore the METAREA forecasts come by SafetyNET, charts by HF weatherfax.

q: You are planning the trade-wind crossing. What wind do you plan for in this square?
a: From the NE, force 5, about half the time
o: From the SW, force 5, about half the time
From the NE, force 1, calm most days
From the E, force 5, nearly all the time
why: Pilot-chart arrows fly with the wind towards the circle: length = frequency (48 %), feathers = mean force (5).

fig.title: Pilot chart, January, 15°N 35°W
lines: Arrows fly with the wind, to the circle
Longest arrow, on the NE side: 48 %

q: Your great-circle route crosses this area. What does the pilot chart tell you to do?
a: Route south of the iceberg limit there
o: Keep the great circle and post a lookout
Keep the great circle: radar shows every berg
Go north of it to shorten the route further
why: The ice limit marks how far south bergs drift that month; growlers hide from radar in a sea and in fog, so route outside it.

fig.title: Halifax to Cork, June
lines: Fog 20 % of the time on the Grand Banks

q: You log the wind and the glass every six hours as a cyclone comes closer, south of the equator. Where are you, and what do you do?
a: Navigable half: run, wind on the port quarter
o: Dangerous half: close-hauled on port tack
Navigable half: run, wind on the starboard quarter
Dangerous half: close-hauled on starboard tack
why: SW → WSW → W turns clockwise, a veer; south of the equator that is the right-hand, navigable half: run, wind on the port quarter.

q: Every three hours you work out the hurricane's bearing from the wind. What do the bearings tell you to do?
a: Navigable half: run with the wind on the starboard quarter
o: Dangerous half: close-hauled, wind on the starboard bow
On its track: run with the wind on the port quarter
Navigable half: run with the wind on the port quarter
why: The centre's bearing moves anticlockwise (096° → 083°): you are left of its track, the navigable half in the north.
ref: Tropical revolving storms — the centre's bearing

fig.title: Hurricane warning, 20°N 62°W
lines: Wind NNW 7, glass falling 1 hPa an hour

q: You plot the cyclone's bearing every three hours. Which heading do you steer now?
a: About 140°, close-hauled on port tack
o: About 040°, close-hauled on starboard tack
About 225°, the wind on the port quarter
About 315°, the wind on the starboard quarter
why: Bearing moving anticlockwise: left half, dangerous in the south. Wind on the port bow: 090° + 50° = 140°, away from the centre.

q: Your crew want to keep going until the typhoon is on the radio. Where is it, and what do you do?
a: About 130°: dangerous half, wind on the starboard bow
o: About 270°: dangerous half, wind on the starboard bow
About 130°: navigable half, wind on the starboard quarter
About 310°: navigable half, wind on the port quarter
why: Face the wind, the centre is about 10 points right: 020° + 112° ≈ 130°, as the swell says. Veering in the north: the dangerous half.
ref: Tropical revolving storms — finding the centre

q: You must choose one of the two courses. Which is it, and how close will the centre pass?
a: 200°: about 150 M off, in the navigable half
o: 020°: about 150 M off, in the navigable half
200°: about 175 M off, in the navigable half
020°: about 175 M off, in the dangerous half
why: Relative motion gives a CPA of about 151 M on either course, in about 19 h; 200° is left of the track, the navigable half.

fig.title: Hurricane plot, 0000 UT, 17°N
lines: Moving 290° at 12 kn, straight at you
You can make 7 kn on 200° or on 020°

q: This Coral Sea cyclone was moving south-west and has now recurved. Which side of it is now the dangerous semicircle?
a: The north-east side, left of the new track
o: The south-east side, as before the turn
The south-west side, right of the new track
The north-west side, behind the centre
why: South of the equator the dangerous half is always left of the track: once the track turns SE, that is the NE side.

q: The forecast says the hurricane will recurve and pass north-west of you. Which way do you go now?
a: South-east, away from the right side of the new track
o: North, to cross ahead of it to its left side
East as planned: it will pass behind you
Heave to and let it pass to the north-west
why: Once it recurves NE you would sit right of the track, the dangerous half: head SE now to open the distance.

fig.title: Hurricane advisory, 1500 UT
lines: You: 33°N 61°W, bound east for the Azores

q: The hurricane has stopped moving. What do you do with the time it gives you?
a: Open the distance now: it may move off any way
o: Stay put: a stalled storm dies where it stands
Close it now to pass behind it while it waits
Heave to and wait until it picks a direction
why: A stalled storm can drift or lurch off in any direction once it is steered again: use the pause to put sea room between you.
ref: Tropical revolving storms — a stalled storm

fig.title: Hurricane advisory, 0900 UT
lines: Centre 250 M east of you, stationary
Your glass and wind steady for 6 h

q: Your crew want to wait for the next advisory in 12 hours. How do you use the boat?
a: Reach for the navigable side now: clear in about 19 h
o: Wait 12 h, then reach: still clear in time
Beat for the dangerous side: clear in about 30 h
Heave to and let her ride it out where she is
why: 150 M at 8 kn ≈ 19 h, inside the 30 h; waiting 12 h first leaves no margin (31 h). A catamaran's speed is her escape.
ref: Tropical revolving storms — a catamaran's options

fig.title: 14 m catamaran, hurricane ahead
lines: Centre crosses your position in 30 h
Clear of 34-kn winds: 150 M off the track
Navigable side: a reach at 8 kn
Dangerous side: a beat at 5 kn

q: You are caught in the storm and this happens. What comes next?
a: The far wall: the wind returns from the SW, as hard
o: The storm has passed: the glass will now rise
It is weakening: the worst of it is over
The wind returns from the NE, but lighter
why: You are in the eye: when it passes, the other wall arrives, with the wind as strong from the opposite direction.

fig.title: Hurricane, 0300
lines: Wind NE 70 kn for the last 4 h

q: It is 1600 in the hurricane season and you correct the reading for the time of day. What do you make of it?
a: 2.0 hPa below normal: under 3, keep logging
o: 3.5 hPa below normal: over 3, suspect a TRS
5.0 hPa below normal: a TRS is near, act now
2.0 hPa below normal: over 1, suspect a TRS
why: Normal at 1600 = 1012 − 1.5 = 1010.5; 1010.5 − 1008.5 = 2.0 hPa. Suspect a TRS at 3 below normal, act at 5.

fig.title: Barometer at 1600 local, 14°N
lines: Pilot chart mean for the month: 1012 hPa

q: Your crew say the afternoon fall is just the daily tide of the barometer. What do the two readings tell you?
a: 5.5 hPa below normal and falling: a TRS is close
o: A 6 hPa fall by 1600 is the normal daily swing
Only 2.5 hPa below normal: the 1600 dip explains it
7.0 hPa below normal: you are inside the storm
why: Normal 1014.5 at 1000, 1011.5 at 1600: 2.5 then 5.5 hPa below. The normal swing is 3 hPa, not 6: a TRS is close.

q: A new swell has been building for two days. What does it tell you?
a: A storm is closing on a steady bearing, about 100°
o: A storm is moving away: the period is falling
A storm lies about 280°, where the swell runs to
Nothing: a swell in the trades means nothing
why: Swell runs out from a storm, so it comes from its bearing; a steady direction, a shorter period and a higher sea: it is coming at you.

q: When did this swell leave the storm that made it?
a: About 70 h ago
o: About 35 h ago
About 105 h ago
About 135 h ago
why: 1.5 × 18 s ≈ 27 kn; 1900 M ÷ 27 kn ≈ 70 h: the swell left the storm about three days ago.
ref: Ocean swell — from a distant storm

fig.title: Anchored at Nuku Hiva, 9°S
lines: New swell from the SSW, period 18 s
Fax: a storm near 40°S, 1900 M away

q: Both swells came from the same distant storm. Roughly how far away was it?
a: About 1130 M
o: About 2270 M
About 760 M
About 570 M
why: 18 s runs at 27 kn, 14 s at 21 kn; the 12-h gap gives D(1/21 − 1/27) = 12, so D ≈ 1130 M.
ref: Ocean swell — from a distant storm

q: You cannot get farther away than this. What wind do you prepare for at the closest point?
a: 34–49 kn: inside the 34-kn radius only
o: 50–63 kn: inside the 50-kn radius
64 kn or more: hurricane force
Under 34 kn: outside every radius
why: 100 M is inside the 160 M of the 34-kn radius but outside the 80 M of the 50-kn one: plan for 34–49 kn, more in gusts.

fig.title: Advisory: Hurricane 'Mara', Cat 2
lines: Forecast closest approach to you: 100 M

q: You plot an advisory with the mariner's 1-2-3 rule, adding 100, 200 and 300 M to the 34-knot radius at 24, 48 and 72 hours. Why does the margin grow?
a: The forecast track error grows with time
o: The storm itself grows as it ages
The storm speeds up as it recurves
Your own DR error grows with time
why: The 100–200–300 M are the average forecast track errors at 24, 48 and 72 h: the further ahead, the less sure the position.

q: Your crew know the South Pacific season runs November to April. What do you tell them about this coast?
a: The South Atlantic almost never breeds them
o: Same season here: November to April
Its season runs June to November
They form, but turn away before Brazil
why: Strong wind shear aloft and no ITCZ south of the equator stop them forming; Catarina (2004) is the only known hurricane.
ref: Tropical revolving storms — where they form

fig.title: Salvador to Rio, February
lines: South Atlantic hurricanes on record: one

q: Planning the leg to the Azores, your crew read the pilot chart like this. What do you tell them?
a: Not quite: rare there in July, not impossible
o: Yes: no storm has ever crossed it in July
Yes: the red lines are this year's forecast
No: the red lines show where storms never go
why: Pilot-chart storm tracks are history for that month: an empty route means storms are rare there, not impossible. Watch the advisories.

fig.title: Pilot chart, North Atlantic, July
lines: Red lines: tracks of past storms
Crew: "So no hurricanes on our route"

q: You compare the two routes on the pilot chart. How many days of gale should each one expect?
a: North about 1.2 days, south about 0.3
o: North about 0.3 days, south about 1.2
North about 1.2 days, south about 3.3
Both about 0.8 days: the miles even it out
why: Gale % is the share of observations at force 8 or more: 8 × 0.15 = 1.2 days north, 11 × 0.03 = 0.33 days south.

fig.title: Pilot chart, May: Bermuda to the Azores

q: You plan the delivery south through the South China Sea. When do you go?
a: December–March, with the NE monsoon behind you
o: June–August, with the SW monsoon behind you
April–May, in the calms between monsoons
September–October, before the NE monsoon sets in
why: On 215° the NE monsoon (Nov–Mar) is a fair wind, and it falls outside the typhoon season; the SW monsoon would be on the nose.

q: You arrive late from Thailand and still want to go west. What do you expect?
a: Calms and squalls, then the SW monsoon on the nose
o: The NE monsoon will return for a few weeks
Steady light easterlies all the way to Oman
The SW monsoon behind you as it sets in
why: Between the monsoons come calms and squalls; the SW monsoon then blows from where you are going. Go west by March, or wait for autumn.

fig.title: Uligan, Maldives, 25 April
lines: Plan: 1300 M west to Salalah, Oman
NE monsoon has died: light, variable
SW monsoon due late May, 25–30 kn

q: You plan to take the boat north up the Red Sea. Which season do you choose?
a: Winter, when SSE winds fill the southern half
o: Summer, when the SW monsoon blows up the sea
Spring, when the northerlies stop for a month
Any season: it blows from the south all year
why: In the NE monsoon (Oct–May) air drawn in from the Gulf of Aden gives SSE winds in the south; in summer NNW blows the whole length.

fig.title: Djibouti to Suez, 1200 M north
lines: North of 20°N: NNW 15–25 kn all year
Gulf of Aden: NE or SW monsoon

q: You join the Puddle Jump fleet from Mexico. Where do you plan to cross the doldrums?
a: Near 125–130°W, where the band is narrower
o: Near 105°W, straight south from Mexico
Near 140°W, just north of Nuku Hiva
Wherever the rhumb line meets the band
why: In March the ITCZ lies a few degrees north of the equator and is wider in the east: sail SW in the NE trade and cross it further west.

fig.title: Puerto Vallarta to Nuku Hiva, late March

q: You plan to motor through the light airs. How much fuel do you allow for them, before any reserve?
a: About 180 L
o: About 450 L
About 60 L
About 1080 L
why: 360 M ÷ 6 kn = 60 h; 60 h × 3 L/h = 180 L, before the reserve.
ref: The ITCZ — Panama to the Galápagos

fig.title: Balboa to San Cristóbal, mid-March
lines: Light airs expected for 360 M of it

q: You planned to sit out the season in French Polynesia. What does the El Niño change?
a: Cyclones form further east: the Tuamotus are at risk
o: Cyclones form further west: the Tuamotus are safer
The season ends early: no cyclones after January
Nothing: El Niño only changes the rainfall
why: In an El Niño the warm water and the cyclones shift east: French Polynesia, usually spared, had several in 1982–83.
ref: El Niño — cyclones and the trades

fig.title: Papeete, Tahiti, October
lines: Season ahead: strong El Niño declared
Plan: the cyclone season in the Tuamotus
Most years: few cyclones east of 150°W

q: The forecasters have declared an El Niño. How does it change the trade-wind passage ahead?
a: Weaker, less steady trades, with more calms
o: Stronger, steadier trades all the way
The trades swing round to the NE
No change: El Niño stays near South America
why: El Niño weakens the Pacific trades, which can even reverse in the west: plan more fuel and a slower passage.
ref: El Niño — cyclones and the trades

fig.title: Galápagos, March, El Niño year
lines: Puddle Jump to the Marquesas, 3000 M

q: The eddy turns like every warm-core ring north of the Gulf Stream. Where do you put the boat?
a: On its east side, where it sets south with you
o: On its west side, where it sets south with you
Through its centre, where the current is strongest
On its east side, where it sets north against you
why: A warm-core ring in the north turns clockwise: its east side sets south, a fair current on 165°.

fig.title: Newport to Bermuda, course 165°
lines: SST chart: an eddy pinched off a meander
its centre 20 M west of your rhumb line

q: Which side of the cold ring gives you a fair current home?
a: Its east side: it turns anticlockwise
o: Its west side: it turns clockwise
Its centre: the current is strongest there
Neither: cold rings carry no current
why: A cold-core ring is a cyclonic eddy, anticlockwise in the north: its east side sets north, fair for 345°.

fig.title: Bermuda to Newport, course 345°
lines: south of the Gulf Stream, 80 M across
Your rhumb line runs through its centre

q: You hold your heading straight across the Stream. How far north-east has it carried you by the time you are out?
a: About 25 M
o: About 50 M
About 17 M
About 8 M
why: 50 M ÷ 6 kn ≈ 8.3 h across; 8.3 h × 3 kn = 25 M set to the NE.
ref: Ocean currents — crossing the Gulf Stream

fig.title: Gulf Stream off Cape Hatteras
lines: You head 135° across it at 6 kn

q: The front's timing has held for two days of forecasts. Do you carry on into the Stream at 0800?
a: Out at 1800, 2 h after the front: wait
o: Out at 1440, ahead of the front: go
Out at 1600, just as the front arrives: go
Out at 1800, but a north wind is harmless: go
why: 60 M ÷ 6 kn = 10 h: in at 0800, out at 1800 — two hours of north wind against a 3-kn current. Wait until the northerly has gone through.

fig.title: Bermuda to Newport, Gulf Stream ahead
lines: Stream 60 M wide, setting NE at 3 kn
You reach its south edge at 0800
Across it at 6 kn over the ground
Front, then N 25 kn, reaches it at 1600

q: Your watch reports this change. Where are you?
a: Just out across the Gulf Stream's north wall
o: Just into the Gulf Stream from the south
In the middle of a warm-core eddy
On the edge of the Grand Banks
why: The Stream's north wall is a sharp drop to the cold slope water: northbound, the sea cools fast and the Stream's chop eases.

q: The south-westerly buster is coming sooner than forecast. Where do you take the boat?
a: Inshore of the 200 m line, out of the current
o: Along the 200 m line, to keep the current's lift
Further out, into the core of the current
Back NE along the 200 m line, running before it
why: A SW gale against the 4-kn current builds the steep, breaking seas of the shelf edge: get out of the stream, inshore.
ref: Ocean currents — the Agulhas and a cold front

fig.title: Agulhas Current, off the Wild Coast
lines: Core on the 200 m line: SW-going, 4 kn
You: on the 200 m line, 60 M from port
SW gale, 40 kn, arriving in 2 h

q: You are riding the Agulhas south-west. What do these signs tell you?
a: A SW buster within hours: make for port
o: The NE will fill in again: carry on
A high is building: the calm will last
A sea breeze is setting in: carry on
why: The NE dies as a coastal low passes; fog and a cloud bank in the SW mean the cold front's SW gale is hours away.
ref: Ocean currents — the Agulhas and a cold front

fig.title: Durban to East London, day 1
lines: NE wind 25 kn, now dying to calm
Glass fell to 1004 hPa, now steady
Fog patches; cloud bank in the SW

q: You are running east at 42°S, and this low will catch you tomorrow. You can alter north or south now. Which do you choose?
a: North, so its centre passes south of you
o: South, so its centre passes north of you
Hold your latitude and let it pass over you
Heave to now until it has gone through
why: South of the equator, north of a low the wind runs NW → W → SW, all fair for the east; south of it, NE → E → SE on the nose.
ref: Southern Ocean — lows and their sequence

q: The front has just gone through. What do you expect over the next day or two?
a: SW easing as a ridge passes, then NW for the next low
o: SW for a week now that the low has stalled
The eye passes next, then NE as hard
SE and a falling glass as the low comes back
why: Southern Ocean lows come in a train: after the cold front the SW eases under a brief ridge, then NW and a falling glass bring the next.
ref: Southern Ocean — lows and their sequence

q: You are eastbound as a depression goes by. Where is its centre passing?
a: South of you, moving east
o: North of you, moving east
Right over you, moving east
South of you, moving west
why: North of the equator a wind that backs (SE → E → NE) under a falling glass means the low's centre is passing south of you.
ref: Depressions — fronts on an ocean crossing

q: Four days out, the GRIB shows the Azores High has shifted. What do you do?
a: Turn east sooner, at about 34°N, in the westerlies
o: Keep north to 38°N, as the plan says
Turn east now, along 31°N
Bear away south of the high for its easterlies
why: The westerlies lie on the high's north side, wherever it is: with the centre at 30°N you find them at 33–34°N, not 38°N.
ref: Subtropical highs — the Azores High's movement

q: The high has moved north-east and is sitting on your destination. How do you plan the passage?
a: Stay north in the westerlies, then motor in
o: Take the rhumb line: the high will move on
Pass south of the centre in its easterlies
Run along 32°N, through the middle of the high
why: Round a northern high the westerlies are on its north side: ride them as far as you can, and carry fuel for the last 300 M of calm.
ref: Subtropical highs — the Azores High's movement

fig.title: Bermuda to Horta, mid-June
lines: Azores High 1035 hPa centred on the Azores
Calms within 300 M of the centre

q: Your crew think a storm is coming. What is this wind?
a: The reinforced winter trades, the 'Christmas winds'
o: A late-season hurricane forming nearby
The ITCZ passing overhead
A cold front's northerly from America
why: In mid-winter a strong Azores–Bermuda High tightens the gradient: the trades blow 25–30 kn for days under clear skies.

fig.title: English Harbour, Antigua, late December
lines: Pilot chart: no TRS in December

q: The funnel is heading your way. What do you do?
a: Steer away across its track and shorten sail
o: Hold on: a waterspout collapses before it arrives
Steer towards it to pass close behind it
Heave to: they never move faster than 5 kn
why: A waterspout moves with its parent cloud and can carry violent winds: alter across its track, reef and close the hatches.

fig.title: Gulf Stream, summer afternoon
lines: Cumulonimbus 2 M to the W, moving E
A funnel dropping from its base to the sea

q: The watch leader wants to keep the spinnaker up until the squall arrives. What do you do?
a: Drop the spinnaker now, before the squall arrives
o: Keep it up and bear away in the gusts
Keep it up until the first rain arrives
Keep it up: squall winds are steadier
why: At night and short-handed, shorten sail before the squall: in 35-kn gusts a spinnaker can broach the boat or be lost.

q: Your crew want to keep full sail: she sails flat and fast. How do you set her up for the night?
a: Reef before dark for the squall gusts, not the mean
o: Full sail: she will heel and warn you in a gust
Full sail, and luff up into each squall
Reef only when the first squall arrives
why: A catamaran does not heel to spill a gust: reef for the 35-kn squall gusts, by true wind, before night falls.

fig.title: 13 m catamaran, trade-wind night
lines: True wind 18 kn, full main and genoa
Builder's chart: first reef at 20 kn true

q: You plot the squall's echo twice. What do you expect?
a: It hits you at about 0300: reef now
o: It hits you at about 0240: reef now
It passes ahead of you at about 0300
It passes astern: the bearing is steady
why: Steady bearing, closing 2 M in 20 min (6 kn): the last 4 M take 40 min, so it reaches you about 0300.

q: The crew trust the GRIB and want full sail all night. Why will it not show the squalls?
a: A squall is smaller than the 15 M grid spacing
o: The file is three hours old by the time it arrives
GRIB files leave out the wind under rain
Squalls form after midnight, past the forecast
why: 0.25° of latitude is 15 M: a model with that spacing averages a 3-M squall away. Set sail for the squalls, not the GRIB.
ref: Weather information — GRIB and its limits

fig.title: GRIB for tonight: GFS, 0.25°
lines: ENE 16–18 kn all night, no change

q: You set the boat up for the night from this file. What do you plan for?
a: Gusts near 28 kn, and more in the squalls
o: A steady 20 kn: the GRIB shows the gusts
20 kn at most: the GRIB is the maximum
Under 20 kn: GRIB files overstate the trades
why: A GRIB gives the mean wind over its grid; gusts run some 40 % higher (20 × 1.4 = 28 kn), and squalls add more.
ref: Weather information — GRIB and its limits

q: You must decide today whether to leave port for a 4-day passage. How do you use the two forecasts?
a: Plan for the worse one and check each new run
o: Average them: about 32 kn at about 1800
Trust GFS: it is updated more often
Ignore both until the front is in sight
why: When the models and the ensemble disagree, confidence is low: plan for the stronger case and watch how each new run moves.
ref: Weather information — GRIB and its limits

fig.title: Two models, front on day 3
lines: ECMWF: front at 0000 next day, 40 kn

q: The chart took hours to reach you. Where along 40°N is the front now?
a: Near 36.7°W
o: Near 40.0°W
Near 37.5°W
Near 33.5°W

q: You have just crossed onto the cold Labrador water over the Grand Banks. What do you prepare for?
a: Thick fog that this wind will not clear
o: Fog only once the wind drops tonight
Clear air: the cold water dries it out
A cold front, with the wind veering NW
why: Warm, moist SW air chilled over the cold Labrador Current gives advection fog: it forms in a breeze and lasts. Radar, AIS, horn.

q: Sailing up the Namibian coast, you log the sea temperature on three stretches. Where do you expect fog?
a: Over B, the only sea colder than the dew point
o: Over A, where the warm sea adds moisture
Over C, within a degree of the dew point
Over all three: this coast is always in fog
why: Fog forms when air is cooled to its dew point: only B (10°C) is below 13°C. The cold Benguela upwelling does this.

fig.title: Lüderitz to Walvis Bay, SE 20 kn
